segments.translit: sahajānandamudito hi bhusukupādas tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati —
segments.translation: Delighted by [innate joy]{sahajananda}, [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as spoken by Bhusukupāda in the delight of innate joy, setting forth 'that same meaning', the formula with which he opens many songs (cp.41.m1).

segments.translit:
āi ityādi | ādau anutpannabhāvatve[58]na jagad idaṃ svayaṃ paramārthajñair avagataṃ tena teṣv anyathābhāvaṃ na gacchati |
tathāgamaḥ —
akāro mukhaṃ sarvvadharmmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt |
atha bhrāntyā vidyātimiralocanān nīlapītādirūpeṇa bho bālayogin bhāvaṃ tvāṃ prati bhāsate |
athācāryyanidattakāḥ —
keśoṇḍakaṃ yathākāśe dṛśyate taimirakair janaiḥ |
tathālokādidoṣeṇa bhāvo bālair vikalpyate ||
atha rajjau(jo) sarpābhijñānaṃ kṛtvā saṃtrāsito yaḥ | so 'pi tena rajju(rājja)sarpeṇa kiṃ satyena khāditaḥ |
segments.translation:
'Āi…' and so on. Those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha} understand this [world]{jagat} for themselves as [non-arising]{anutpada} in nature from the start; so, for them, it does not become otherwise. So [scripture]{agama} says:
'The [letter a]{akara} is the door to all [dharmas]{dharma}, because they are [non-arising]{anutpada} from the beginning.'
But through [confusion]{bhranti}, O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, a thing appears to you in the form of blue, yellow and so on, from an eye with the [dim sight]{dim-sight} of [ignorance]{avidya}. As the teacher [Nidattaka]{p-nidattaka} says:
'As people with [dim sight]{dim-sight} see a [tangle of hairs]{kesonduka} in the sky,
so, through the fault of light and the like, a thing is fashioned by fools in [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.'
And one who has taken a rope for a [snake]{snake} and is terrified: is he truly bitten by that [rope-snake]{rajjusarpa}?
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 1 as a contrast: those who know the ultimate understand the world as non-arising from the start, while the novice yogin, through confusion and the dim sight of ignorance, sees things as blue, yellow and so on, like someone terrified by a rope taken for a snake, who is not truly bitten (cp.41.m2).

citations.work: Unnamed 'scripture' (āgama). The formula opens the arapacana syllabary of the Large Perfection of Wisdom sūtras (e.g. the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā), from which it was widely quoted; the exact source Munidatta drew on is not given.

citations.quoted: keśoṇḍakaṃ yathākāśe dṛśyate taimirakair janaiḥ | tathālokādidoṣeṇa bhāvo bālair vikalpyate ||
citations.work: Attributed by Munidatta to the ācārya Nidattaka (form of the name uncertain; Tibetan slob dpon ni dA ta kA); no work is named.

flags.note: Printed bhrāntyā vidyātimiralocanān, 'through confusion, from an eye with the dim sight of knowledge', makes no sense; read avidyā-, 'ignorance'. The word division is the editor's: bhrāntyā + avidyā- joins by sandhi to bhrāntyāvidyā-, so the written text allows either division, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'khrul pa ma rig pa ... rab rib can gyi mig gis, 'confusion, ignorance ... by the eye with dim sight'. The translation reads avidyā and links 'ignorance', not the 'vidya' entry. -locanān is -locanāt by sandhi before nīla-.

For svayaṃ paramārthajñair, 'by those who know the ultimate, for themselves', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang dang gzhan don shes pas, 'by knowing one's own and others' aims': it reads paramārtha as para-artha, 'others' aim' (gzhan don), with rang, 'one's own', apparently for svayam. It also takes anutpannabhāva- as 'things being unborn' (dngos po rnams ma skyes pa nyid kyis). I follow the Sanskrit.

In the Tibetan the novice yogin is the agent: kye'i byis pa'i rnal 'byor pas dngos po nyid du shes so, 'O, the novice yogin knows it as a real thing', where the Sanskrit has the thing appear to him (bhāvaṃ tvāṃ prati bhāsate, with accusative bhāvaṃ for the expected nominative bhāvaḥ). The Tibetan has nag po, 'black', for nīla, 'blue, dark'. Its lemma dbang po, 'faculty, lord', is apparently a slip for dang po, 'first', as in its line 1a (dang po ma skyes pa nyid kyis).

The teacher is printed athācāryyanidattakāḥ (honorific plural), the Tibetan slob dpon ni dA ta kAs. Since ni is also the ordinary Tibetan topic particle, the Tibetan may name him simply dA ta ka (Dattaka?), and the Sanskrit ni- may then have another source. Linked to the proposed p-nidattaka; the form of the name is uncertain. The verse's wording resembles Mahāyāna sūtra verses on the hair-net seen by those with dim sight (perhaps the Laṅkāvatāra); I have not checked.

The Tibetan sets the rope-snake sentence (atha rajjau ... khāditaḥ) as four lines of verse, as if it continued Nidattaka's quotation; the Sanskrit reads as Munidatta's prose paraphrase of 1b, echoing its words (dekhi > abhijñāna, camakii > saṃtrāsita, khāi > khādita) (cp.41.m2). The manuscript's rājja- (in Shastri's parentheses) for rajju- echoes the song's rājasāpa and supports taking that word as 'rope-snake'. Khādita is literally 'eaten'; 'bitten' follows the draft's 1b, and the Tibetan has rmug, 'bite'.

The folio mark [58] falls inside the word anutpannabhāvatve[58]na; it is not Munidatta's wording and is not translated. Ālokādidoṣa is taken in the ordinary sense, 'the fault of light and the like' (poor light, as when a rope is seen as a snake); the Tibetan snang sogs nyes pa, 'fault of appearance and the rest', uses the word that also renders the technical āloka of the completion stage, which seems not to be meant, so 'light' is not linked.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha —
akaṭetyādi | ākaṭāścaryyaṃ bho bālayogin atra hastāmarṣaṃ mā kuru | īdṛśasvabhāvena yadi jagatsvarūpāvagamaṃ karoṣi tadā anādibhavavikalpavāsanādoṣasaṃgrahaṃ palāyate tava |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he states the [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}: 'Akaṭa…' and so on. Ākaṭa: a [wonder]{adbhuta}. O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, do not grope here with your hands. If you understand the [true nature]{svarupa} of the [world]{jagat} as being of such a [nature]{svabhava}, then the accumulated faults of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} in beginningless [existence]{bhava} flee from you.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the refrain as praise of the path. He glosses akaṭa as 'a wonder' and tells the novice yogin not to grope here with his hands: once he understands the world's true nature to be such, the faults of the habitual tendencies of conceptual thought, gathered through beginningless existence, flee (cp.41.m3).

flags.note: Hastāmarṣa: āmarṣa as printed means 'impatience, anger'; read āmarśa, 'touching' (from ā-mṛś), the manuscript writing ṣ for ś as elsewhere (sū(śū)citaḥ in cp.41.m5). 'Touching with the hand' supports the draft's 2a 'grope with your hands'. The Tibetan line and comment have lag pas sgre ba, apparently 'feel about with the hand', though the comment softens the prohibition to 'there is no need' (mi dgos).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) glosses ngo mtshar as 'counted a wonder' (mtshar du brtsis), matching ākaṭa = āścaryya. It renders īdṛśasvabhāvena as 'by such a thing' ('di 'dra'i dngos pos), turns the condition into a command ('realize the nature of beings!'), and takes saṃgraha as 'what you have grasped' (khyod kyis ... gzung ba rnams).

-saṃgrahaṃ is accusative where palāyate, 'flees', wants a nominative subject; the sense is clear. The commentary's 'flees' stands where the song's 2b has tuṭa, 'is broken': a difference of wording, not of reading, so the draft's 'broken' stands.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārthaṃ saṃvṛttidṛṣṭāntena spaṣṭayati —
marumarīcītyādi | mṛgatṛṣṇāgandharvvanagaradarśanādi pratibhāsamātraṃ bhāvasya yogivareṇa [59ka] dṛśyate |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
yathā māyā yathā svapnaṃ tathāsmi hy antarābhavam ityādi ||
etat sarvvavidyāvāsanādoṣeṇa mithyā bālair vikalpyate | yathā vātāvarttena nīram api prastaraṃ bhūtaṃ tadvat bhāvagrāmo yogīndreṇa boddhavyaḥ |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
śūnyataiva bhaved bhāvo vāsanāvāsitā satī |
vātāvartte dṛḍhībhūtā āpa eva ghanopalāḥ ||
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he makes the same point plain through examples of the [conventional]{samvrti}: 'Marumarīci…' and so on. As in seeing a [mirage]{marici}, a [city of the gandharvas]{gandharvanagara} and the like, the best of [yogis]{yogi} sees only the mere [appearance]{abhasa} of a thing. And so [scripture]{agama} says:
'As an [illusion]{maya}, as a [dream]{svapna}, so is the [intermediate existence]{antarabhava},' and so on.
All this is falsely fashioned by fools in [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}, through the fault of the [habitual tendencies]{vasana} of [ignorance]{avidya}. As even water has become [stone]{stone} through a [whirlwind]{vatavarta}, so the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} should understand the [host of things]{bhavagrama}. And so [scripture]{agama} says:
'[Emptiness]{sunyata} itself, perfumed by [habitual tendencies]{vasana}, would become a thing,
as water itself, made firm in a [whirlwind]{vatavarta}, becomes hailstones.'
segments.note: Munidatta says couplet 3 makes the same point through examples of conventional truth: the best of yogis sees things as mere appearance, like a mirage or a city of the gandharvas, while fools construct them through tendencies of ignorance. As a whirlwind turns water to stone, emptiness perfumed by habitual tendencies becomes a thing (cp.41.m4).

citations.quoted: yathā māyā yathā svapnaṃ tathāsmi hy antarābhavam…
citations.work: Unnamed 'scripture' (āgama); probably the Hevajra Tantra, whose verse I recall as 'yathā māyā yathā svapnaṃ yathā syād antarābhavam / tathaiva maṇḍalaṃ bhāti…' (unchecked).

citations.quoted: śūnyataiva bhaved bhāvo vāsanāvāsitā satī | vātāvartte dṛḍhībhūtā āpa eva ghanopalāḥ ||

flags.note: Printed etat sarvvavidyāvāsanādoṣeṇa, 'all this ... through the fault of the tendencies of knowledge'; read avidyā-, 'ignorance' (sarvāvidyā- or sarvam avidyā-), with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) de thams cad ma rig pa'i bag chags kyi skyon gyis, 'all that, by the fault of the tendencies of ignorance'. The avidya entry already lists the parallel compound anādyavidyāvāsanādoṣeṇa. Not linked to 'vidya'.

Tathāsmi hy antarābhavam, 'so I am indeed the intermediate existence', is hard to construe; perhaps read tathāsti, 'so is' (Bengali স্ম and স্ত are easily confused). The Tibetan has de bzhin du ni bar srid do, 'so is the intermediate existence', which the translation follows. If the verse is the Hevajra's (see citations), its known form is different again (yathā syād antarābhavam).

The Tibetan takes saṃvṛtti adverbially ('makes it clear by example, conventionally', kun rdzob tu dpe yis); renders pratibhāsamātra as 'mere reflection' (gzugs brnyan tsam); expands bālaiḥ, 'by fools', to 'by novice yogins' (byis pa'i rnal 'byor pa rnams kyis); and renders bhāvagrāma, 'host of things', as dngos po'i grong khyer, 'city of things', taking grāma as 'village, town'.

In the Tibetan of the last verse, emptiness is 'perfumed by the tendencies of things' (dngos po'i bag chags kyis bsgos), and the last line reads chu yis de nyid tshogs pa 'bros, 'by water that very mass flees', apparently taking ghanopalāḥ, 'hailstones', as ghana, 'mass', with a form of palāy-, 'flee'. The Sanskrit simile, water made firm in a whirlwind becoming hailstones, is clear and is followed. The folio mark [59ka] after yogivareṇa is not translated.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadenātyantābhāvaṃ sūcayati —
vāndhītyādi | vaṃdhyā bhāgavatī nairātmā tasyāḥ sutaḥ paramārthasatyaṃ bālukātailopamaṃ śaśaśṛ(sṛ)ṅgopamaṃ ca | etenānutpannasvabhāvo hi tasya sū(śū)citaḥ | sa eva utpanno hi paramārthasatya[ṃ] mahāsukhapañcajñānātmakaḥ jagati nānāprakāreṇa krīḍārasam anubhavatīti |
tathā ca sūtake —
pañcabuddhyātmakasarvvajago 'yam ityādi |
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he points to [absolute nonexistence]{atyantabhava}: 'Vāndhi…' and so on. The [barren]{barren} woman is the [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. Her son is [ultimate]{paramartha} truth, like [oil from sand]{valukataila} and like a [hare's horn]{sasasrnga}. By this its [non-arising]{anutpada} [nature]{svabhava} is pointed out. He himself, arisen, the [ultimate]{paramartha} truth made of [great bliss]{mahasukha} and the [five wisdoms]{pancajnana}, enjoys the flavour of [play]{lila} in the [world]{jagat} in many ways. And so in the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}:
'This whole world has the nature of the five [buddhas]{buddha},' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 4 as pointing to absolute nonexistence. The barren woman is the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, selflessness as a goddess, as in song 33 (cp.33.m4); her son is ultimate truth, unarisen like oil from sand or a hare's horn, yet, made of great bliss and the five wisdoms, he plays in the world (cp.41.m5).

equations.src: vaṃdhyā (the song's bām̐ddhi), the barren woman
tasyāḥ sutaḥ (the song's suā), her son

citations.work: Sūtaka, named by Munidatta (also cited on song 13); not otherwise identified.

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has sa eva utpanno hi, 'he himself, arisen', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de rnams skye ba med pa'i phyir, 'because they are unborn'. Either the Tibetan read anutpanna (or smoothed the paradox), or the Sanskrit means the paradox, the unarisen son 'arisen' and at play, as the song's barren woman's son plays. The hiatus eva utpanno is irregular sandhi. I translate the Sanskrit; the reviewer should decide. The Tibetan also has 'the bliss of play' (rol pa'i bde ba) for krīḍārasa, 'the flavour of play'.

Printed bhāgavatī is taken as bhagavatī, 'Blessed Lady' (Tibetan bcom ldan 'das). Pañcabuddhyātmaka- is read -buddhātmaka-, 'having the nature of the five buddhas', with the Tibetan sangs rgyas lnga bdag; jagaḥ stands for jagat. Sū(śū)citaḥ and śaśaśṛ(sṛ)ṅga follow Shastri's corrections (the manuscript's spellings in parentheses), and paramārthasatya[ṃ] his restoration; the masculine -ātmakaḥ agrees with sa, not with the neuter satyam.
Munidatta names oil from sand and the hare's horn but not the sky-flower of 4b, and he does not gloss the 'many games' beyond saying the son enjoys the flavour of play in many ways (cp.41.m5).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena bhāvapariśuddhim āha —
bhusuku ityādi | bhusukupādo hi vadati bhāva[ā]nām eṣa rūpo hi mayā kathitaḥ | bho bālayogin yadi [60] tava bhrāntir atrāsti tadā sadgurucaraṇārādhanaṃ kuru || 41 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the complete purity of things: 'Bhusuku…' and so on. [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says: 'This is the form of things, told by me.' O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, if you have [confusion]{bhranti} about this, then worship the feet of the true [guru]{guru}.
segments.note: Munidatta says the last couplet states the purity of things. Passing over Rāutu, he has Bhusukupāda alone say 'this form of things has been told by me'. His wording implies one speaker, as if Rāutu were Bhusuku's title, and supports kaṭa as 'told'. His 'worship the true guru's feet' supports pāba as 'feet' (cp.41.m6).

flags.note: Rāutu: Munidatta's lemma begins at bhusuku, and his paraphrase has a single speaker, 'Bhusukupāda says: this form of things has been told by me' (singular vadati, first-person mayā kathitaḥ) (cp.41.m6). He thus does not treat Rāutu as a second speaker; his wording fits Rāutu (Old Bengali rāuta, 'prince') as a title of Bhusuku, the two halves of 5a saying the same thing, though his silence could also mean he simply skipped the name. The Tibetan comment likewise names only Bhusuku ('du shes gsum pa) and has 'explained by me' (bdag gis bshad pa); the Tibetan line transcribes rA u ta in unclear syntax (rA u ta yi dam gtam b+hu su ku). Mayā kathitaḥ supports the draft's kaṭa as 'told'.

Pāba (5b): Munidatta's sadgurucaraṇārādhanaṃ kuru, 'worship the true guru's feet', has 'feet' (caraṇa), which supports reading pāba as 'feet' (from pāda) rather than 'you will obtain' (cp.41.m6). But he puts 'worship' (ārādhana) where the song has pucchatu, 'ask', and caraṇa beside guru is a set honorific, so the support is limited. The Tibetan line has bla ma dam pa'i zhabs la dri bar gyis, 'ask at the true guru's feet', and its comment zhabs la gus par bya, 'be devoted to the feet'; neither has 'obtain'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders bhāvapariśuddhi as 'complete purity of own-nature' (ngo bo nyid yongs su dag pa) and bhāvānām eṣa rūpaḥ as 'the own-nature of things' (dngos po rnams kyi ... ngo bo nyid). Rūpa here means 'nature, character' (and is irregularly masculine), so it is not linked to the glossary's 'form' (visible form). Bhāva[ā]nām is Shastri's restoration; the folio mark [60] after yadi and the closing song number 41 are not translated.

proposals.definition: The host or mass of things (Sanskrit bhāvagrāma; grāma is 'village', also 'collection'): everything that exists, taken together. Munidatta tells the lord of yogis to understand it as water turned to stone by a whirlwind (cp.41.m4); elsewhere he speaks of its force (cp.12.m5) and its appearance (cp.29.m5). The Tibetan has dngos po'i grong khyer, 'city of things'.
proposals.rationale: Recurs in the commentary (cp.12.m5, cp.29.m5, cp.41.m4) and is already rendered 'host of things' inside the bhavabala, udakacandra and vatavarta entries; an entry of its own keeps the rendering and the Tibetan 'city of things' consistent.

questions: Nidattaka (cp.41.m2): the Sanskrit has athācāryyanidattakāḥ, the Tibetan slob dpon ni dA ta kAs. If ni is the Tibetan topic particle, the Tibetan names him dA ta ka (Dattaka?). Should the proposed p-nidattaka keep 'Nidattaka', and its Tibetan form be ni dA ta kA or dA ta ka?

Avidyā for printed vidyā- at cp.41.m2 (bhrāntyā vidyātimira-, which sandhi allows to be divided bhrāntyāvidyā-) and cp.41.m4 (sarvvavidyāvāsanā-), both backed by the Tibetan ma rig pa. Do you accept the emendation? If so, the dim-sight entry's form vidyātimiralocanān might be noted as avidyā-, and the avidya entry could gain both forms.

Bhāva, 'a thing' (cp.41.m2, m4, m6), is left unlinked: bhava-being's 'being' reads here as 'a living being', and bhava-abhava's 'being and nonbeing' does not fit. Add 'thing' as a variant of bhava-being, or keep it unlinked?
I propose bhavagrama, 'host of things' (cp.12.m5, cp.29.m5, cp.41.m4), and use it in cp.41.m4. Accept, or fold it into an existing entry?
Cp.41.m5: the Sanskrit has the son 'arisen' (sa eva utpanno), the Tibetan 'unborn' (skye ba med pa). I translated the Sanskrit as a deliberate paradox; should it be emended to anutpanno?

Cp.41.m4: I read tathāsmi as tathāsti, 'so is', with the Tibetan. Can you confirm whether the verse is the Hevajra's (yathā māyā yathā svapnaṃ yathā syād antarābhavam…)? I quote that form from memory.

Song line 5a: Munidatta passes over Rāutu and has Bhusuku alone speak, 'told by me' (cp.41.m6). I suggest leaving the draft line as it is, with a note that Munidatta treats the couplet as one speaker's words, so Rāutu may be Bhusuku's title (rāuta, 'prince'), while the Tibetan transcribes it as a name. Do you want that note, or a stronger claim?

Song line 5b: Munidatta's 'the true guru's feet' and the Tibetan line's zhabs la dri bar gyis both support pāba as 'feet' (cp.41.m6), so the draft's 'ask at the feet of the true guru' looks right; but Munidatta has 'worship' for 'ask'. Is a note on the 'you will obtain' alternative still wanted?
To keep the approved English for vikalpa where Munidatta uses the verb (vikalpyate, cp.41.m2 and m4), I wrote 'fashioned ... in conceptual thought'. Would you prefer a plain 'imagined', unlinked?

Equations list only the explicit equations (ākaṭa = wonder; the barren woman = Nairātmā; her son = ultimate truth). The Sanskrit synonyms Munidatta substitutes for song words (marumarīci > mṛgatṛṣṇā, pāthara > prastara, khāi > khādita) are not listed. Should they be?
